facts.fact: Accelerated industrialization of the El Salto industrial corridor (El Salto, Juanacatlán, Poncitlán, Ocotlán), later extending to Tlajomulco and Ixtlahuacán de los Membrillos with NAFTA-era investment: chemical, petrochemical, metal-mechanic, textile, automotive, electronics, pharmaceutical and food plants.
facts.title: An industrial corridor grows on the river

facts.fact: PROFEPA registered 159 industries discharging wastewater to the Río Santiago (Ocotlán area and two corridors); CONAGUA counted 280 discharges, 266 of them into the Santiago.
facts.title: 159 industries, 280 discharges
facts.place: Río Santiago, Ocotlán to El Salto

facts.img_credit: Pollution foam on the Río Santiago in the Barranca de Huentitán, downstream of Guadalajara, April 2024. Photo: Mtenaespinoza, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

facts.fact: IMTA study for CEA Jalisco (sampling Mar 2009–May 2010) detected 1,090 toxic substances, chemicals and metals in discharges and river water; 87–94% of industries failed at least one NOM-001-SEMARNAT-1996 parameter, and industrial discharges were more polluting than municipal ones.
facts.title: 1,090 toxic substances detected

facts.img_credit: Pollution foam on the Río Santiago in the Barranca de Huentitán, downstream of Guadalajara, April 2024. Photo: Mtenaespinoza, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

facts.fact: Miguel Ángel López Rocha (8–9 years old) fell into the Río Santiago/El Ahogado canal at El Salto on 25 Jan 2008 and died on 13 Feb 2008; hospital notes diagnosed arsenic poisoning. CNDH Recommendation 12/2010 (2 Mar 2010) faulted CONAGUA for failing to enforce environmental norms.
facts.title: A boy dies after falling into the river
facts.place: Arroyo El Ahogado at El Salto

facts.fact: An IMTA June 2008 monitoring report (cited by CNDH 12/2010) concluded the main source of Santiago pollution is water from Arroyo El Ahogado; Puente Grande showed significant acute toxicity attributed to heavy metals.
facts.title: El Ahogado: the main source

facts.img_credit: The old bridge at Puente Grande (Tololotlán), Tonalá, over the Río Santiago, 2018. Photo: Alejandro Hernández Osuna, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

facts.fact: Jalisco human rights commission (CEDHJ) issued Macro-Recomendación 1/2009 with 100 points addressed to the governor, 14 municipalities, SIAPA and CEA.
facts.title: 100-point state human-rights recommendation
facts.img_alt: Pollution foam on the Río Santiago in the Barranca de Huentitán, downstream of Guadalajara, April 2024.
facts.img_credit: Pollution foam on the Río Santiago in the Barranca de Huentitán, downstream of Guadalajara, April 2024. Photo: Mtenaespinoza, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

facts.fact: Greenpeace/UCCS/Un Salto de Vida study: >90% of residents of El Salto, Juanacatlán and Ocotlán live within 5 km of the Santiago, El Ahogado or Zula; 51% (El Salto) and 81% (Juanacatlán) live within 1 km. Mortality from hypertensive kidney disease and renal failure rose in El Salto and Juanacatlán in 2007–2010.
facts.title: Living next to the river
facts.img_alt: The riverside in Juanacatlán, with water hyacinth on the Río Santiago and El Salto across the river, August 2024.
facts.img_credit: The riverside in Juanacatlán, with water hyacinth on the Río Santiago and El Salto across the river, August 2024. Photo: José González Peña, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

facts.fact: The same study listed the 10 facilities with the highest RETC-reported heavy-metal and cyanide discharges (2004–2009): CIBA (now Huntsman), Grupo Celanese, Cervecería Modelo de Guadalajara, Nestlé México, Hilasal Mexicana, Cervecería Cuauhtémoc Moctezuma, Casa Cuervo, IBM de México, Servicios Estrella Azul de Occidente (only 9 names are printed).
facts.title: The ten biggest metal and cyanide dischargers

facts.img_credit: Pollution foam on the Río Santiago in the Barranca de Huentitán, downstream of Guadalajara, April 2024. Photo: Mtenaespinoza, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

facts.fact: A UASLP study commissioned by CEA (2009–2010) of ~300 children found high exposure to lead, arsenic, cadmium, mercury, benzene and POPs in El Salto, Juanacatlán, La Cofradía and Puente Grande; results were kept secret for years. CEDHJ found rights violations by CEA and health authorities (June 2022).
facts.title: Children exposed to metals and benzene

facts.fact: At the El Salto–Juanacatlán waterfall the polluted, sulfate-rich water churns into thick foam that wind carries onto the bridge and homes; residents report headaches, nausea and eye irritation.
facts.title: Toxic foam at the falls
facts.img_alt: Heaps of toxic foam on the Río Santiago at Huentitán, downstream of the Juanacatlán falls, April 2024.
facts.img_credit: Heaps of toxic foam on the Río Santiago at Huentitán, downstream of the Juanacatlán falls, April 2024. Photo: Mtenaespinoza, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

facts.fact: All urban drains flow into the El Salto–Juanacatlán diversion dam; foam bubbles 15–50 cm in diameter rise from the falls and drift onto passers-by and neighbours.
facts.title: Every city drain ends at the falls
facts.img_alt: The Salto de Juanacatlán falls and the old mill and power plant, in a historic photo from before the pollution.
facts.img_credit: The Salto de Juanacatlán falls and the old mill and power plant, in a historic photo from before the pollution. Photo: Eimolinac, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

facts.fact: UN Working Group on Business and Human Rights members visited the falls in 2016 and called it "una catástrofe ecológica"; Greenpeace sampling the same year found nonylphenols, phthalates and bisphenol-A in treated effluent of PTAR El Ahogado.
facts.title: "An ecological catastrophe"

facts.img_credit: The Salto de Juanacatlán falls and the old mill and power plant, in a historic photo from before the pollution. Photo: Eimolinac, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

facts.fact: PROFEPA Recommendation PFPA/1/2C.5/03/2017 to upstream Lerma states (Durango, Guanajuato, Edomex, Michoacán, Nayarit, Querétaro, Zacatecas): the Lerma–Santiago basin shows arsenic, cyanide, mercury, benzene, vinyl chloride, lead, cadmium, chromium and other contaminants — pollution also arrives from the Lerma via Lake Chapala.
facts.title: Pollution also arrives from the Lerma

facts.fact: Chronic kidney disease has been reported since the early 1990s on the Lake Chapala shore, with most cases in San Pedro Itzicán and Agua Caliente (Poncitlán); authorities attribute it to multiple factors and have not established a causal link to water pollution.
facts.title: Kidney disease on the Chapala shore
facts.place: San Pedro Itzicán and Agua Caliente

facts.fact: RENAMECA data reviewed by CNDH: Santiago water was "strongly contaminated" for fecal coliforms at all 9 study sites and "contaminated" for DQO at almost all; high Vibrio fischeri toxicity at the site before Nestlé (Ocotlán) and after Arroyo El Ahogado.
facts.title: Fecal coliforms at every site

facts.img_credit: Pollution foam on the Río Santiago in the Barranca de Huentitán, downstream of Guadalajara, April 2024. Photo: Mtenaespinoza, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

facts.fact: In CONAGUA's 2025 semáforo, every site with 2025 data on the Santiago from Ocotlán to Puente Grande, on Arroyo El Ahogado and on the Zula is RED (failing DQO and fecal coliforms/E. coli; Vibrio toxicity at El Ahogado sites); on the Lerma near Chapala 5 of 6 sites with 2025 data are red and one yellow.
facts.title: Every 2025 station on the Santiago is red
facts.img_credit: The Río Lerma at Ocotlán, 2017. Photo: Sahagun, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

facts.fact: The Santiago basin in Jalisco (6.29 M people) generates ~13,400 L/s of wastewater; 68 PTARs treat 9,926 L/s (74%), up from 7,764 L/s in 2018. Hydrogen sulfide at the El Salto–Juanacatlán dam fell from 10.82 to 9.10 mg/L after solar recirculators were installed.
facts.title: 74% of wastewater treated

facts.fact: CEA reported 103 wastewater and industrial discharges into the Río Santiago found by 40 CONAGUA inspectors; polluted water reached the Las Pintas system and the Miravalle water-treatment plant intake.
facts.title: 103 discharges found; drinking-water intake reached
facts.img_alt: Presa Las Pintas, the reservoir on the Las Pintas sewage canal, El Salto, 2010.

story.title: Lerma into Chapala
text: The Lerma drains the industrial Bajío and ends in Lake Chapala, Mexico’s largest lake (≈1100 km², 7 m average depth, Ramsar site 1973).

Guadalajara pumps about 60% of its drinking water from here (6.65 m³/s in 2025, SIAPA/PIA) through the 1991 Chapala–Guadalajara aqueduct and the older Atequiza–Las Pintas canal system. The lake sits in watershed 1217 Río Lerma 7, which CONAGUA lists in deficit (−250.7 hm³/yr).

story.title: Ocotlán: the Santiago is born
text: The Río Santiago leaves the lake at Ocotlán. For decades the lake has released little water, so the first kilometres mostly carry the Río Zula and local wastewater.
Ocotlán and Poncitlán host food, chemical and furniture plants. Red dots are CONAGUA stations that fail the federal traffic-light (fecal coliforms, COD, toxicity).

story.title: The El Salto corridor
text: Since the 1970s an industrial corridor of chemical, textile, electronics, automotive and food plants has grown along the river between Ocotlán and El Salto. Magenta circles are facilities that reported pollutant releases to water or sewer to SEMARNAT’s RETC; size is cumulative kg 2004–2022.

The Arroyo El Ahogado and Canal Las Pintas bring south-metro sewage and industrial effluent into the river just above the Juanacatlán falls, where hydrogen sulfide and toxic foam drift over El Salto and Juanacatlán. In 2008 a boy, Miguel Ángel López Rocha, died after falling into the river here (CNDH Rec. 12/2010).

story.title: Guadalajara’s buried rivers
text: The city was built over the Atemajac valley. The Río San Juan de Dios has been piped since 1909 under Calzada Independencia; the Atemajac, Osorio and Río Blanco carry the city’s storm and wastewater north and east into the barranca.

Two macro-plants, Agua Prieta (8.5 m³/s design, 2014) and El Ahogado, now treat much of the metro wastewater, but both still discharge to the Santiago and Agua Prieta needs upgrading to meet NOM-001-SEMARNAT-2021.

story.title: Barranca de Huentitán
text: A canyon about 600 m deep on Guadalajara’s northern edge, protected since 2016 as a state natural area (≈21,383 ha with the Río Verde canyon). It holds 368 wild vertebrate species.

The river at its bottom collects the metro’s wastewater. The Arcediano dam, planned here to supply the city, was suspended in 2009 after the village was displaced, partly because the water was too contaminated to treat.

story.title: Dams and the Pacific
text: Below the Verde confluence the Santiago crosses Santa Rosa, La Yesca, El Cajón and Aguamilpa dams before reaching the Pacific north-west of San Blas, Nayarit, after 562 km. CONAGUA estimates mean natural runoff of 7,349 hm³/yr.

Severe contamination is documented in the Jalisco reach (El Salto-Juanacatlan to Arcediano). Evidence that it is detectable at Aguamilpa exists from 1992-1997 monitoring (organic pollution indicators, nitrogen/phosphorus above ecological criteria); no recent peer-reviewed study of the Nayarit estuary/coast was found. The mouth borders Marismas Nacionales (Ramsar 732), one of the Pacific’s largest mangrove systems.

chapala.intro: Lake Chapala is the main source for the Guadalajara metro (≈60% of SIAPA supply; PIA documents say the aqueduct serves >60% of the population). Its level falls ~0.7–1.5 m each dry season (evaporation + extraction) and recovers in the rainy season with Lerma inflows; lows in 1955, 1990–91 and 2001–02 drove the 1991 aqueduct and the search for the Calderón/Zapotillo sources. It is also a Ramsar wetland (site 1973).
chapala.series_note: Yearly dry-season minimum and rainy-season maximum, CEA gauge scale (cota 97.80 ≈ 1,523.8 m a.s.l.). 1900–2021 and 2024–2026 from CEA Jalisco; 2022–23 are spot readings from press/UdeG.
notes: Guadalajara’s concession is 240 hm³/yr (7.61 m³/s). Actual extraction in 2025: 6.65 m³/s, 60.2% of SIAPA supply.
SIAPA supply by source, 2025: Chapala 60.2%, Calderón/Río Verde 17.2%, wells 22.6% (total 11.05 m³/s).

The lake drops about 0.7–1.5 m each dry season through evaporation and extraction, and recovers with Lerma inflows in the rains. The lows of 1955, 1990–91 and 2001–02 pushed the city to build the 1991 aqueduct and to seek water from Calderón and El Zapotillo.
